proposals.relationship: Maruyama recalls using Marx’s inversion of Hegel as a conceptual analogy for Norinaga’s transformation of Sorai’s thought, then changing the wording after Nanbara warned about its political resonance.
proposals.evidence_note: Own August1974retrospective author introductionxviii explicitly identifies the analogy and Marx’s criticism of Hegel in the preface to the second edition of Capital. This is a particular interpretive/metaphorical resource, not a general profession of Marxist identity. Translation of this introduction is Ronald P.Dore, distinct from Hane’s main-book translation. Original Japanese essay, German Marx passage and unrevised manuscript unread; the claim is Maruyama’s later testimony, not independent proof of a1930sreading sequence.

proposals.relationship: Maruyama names Weber among the writers who supplied occasional hints for his study of the transition from natural to artificial social order in Tokugawa political thought.
proposals.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxix expressly denies any single obvious influence on the PartIIleitmotif while naming Weber alongside Ferdinand Tönnies and Ernst Troeltsch. Scope is exactly these occasional hints, not an exclusive source or derivation of all Maruyama’s rationalization theory. Hane’s separate translator prefaceviiialso reports Maruyama’s position between historicism and empiricism through Weber/Heller/Mannheim, quoting the1963introduction, which remains unread here. Main evidence is own1974retrospective translated by Dore; original Weber works and PartIIchapters unread.

proposals.relationship: Maruyama credits Marxist attention to social context and class structure, and Borkenau’s analysis of changing thought categories, as methodological resources for linking the internal development of ideas to social history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxiv–xxviandxxvii–xxviiiis explicit about his methodological stimuli and refusal to treat culture/philosophy as self-sufficient. Borkenau is a specifically named resource for nature/reason/law and the norm/nature split, not a synonym for all Marxists or automatic Frankfurt-School affiliation. The group endpoint is Marxist social history; Karl Marx’s particular analogy is separately proposed. Own remarks deny exclusive adherence to any school. Borkenau original and original Japanese texts unread; Dore translation retained.

proposals.relationship: Maruyama criticizes Marxist intellectual histories that reduce ideas to class reflections or fail to explain concretely the relation between ideas’ internal logic and changes in the social base, while retaining sympathy for scholars working under repression.
proposals.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxiii–xxviiidifferentiates simplistic orthodox-Soviet reductions from more sophisticated Japanese approaches, then objects to unresolved mediation, progressive/reactionary sorting and inferences about popular thought from rebellion records. He also credits scholars’ conscience and anti-authoritarian constraints; this is not rejection of every Marxist method or attribution of all objections directly to Marx. Broad group criticism is distinct from own positive resources and the Karl Marx analogy. Retrospective August1974text translated by Dore; specific criticized originals unread.
